title: NFC Dry Inlays — Adhesive-Free PET for Lamination
summary: NFC dry inlays are bare chip-and-antenna assemblies on 50 µm PET film with no adhesive layer and no release liner — the inlay-stage flagship product for card bureaus, key-fob manufacturers, wristband converters and injection-mould integrators. Survives standard PVC card lamination 140-150 °C / 200-300 psi / 15-25 minute dwell on Bürkle / Wickert / Agfa hydraulic platen presses. Polycarbonate-grade variant for high-security ID cards (160-180 °C). Available with the full NXP HF chip range. NTAG213/215/216, MIFARE Classic 1K/4K, MIFARE DESFire EV2/EV3, MIFARE Ultralight C/EV1, ICODE SLIX2 — plus prelam sheet service that eliminates one lamination step on high-speed lines.
heroPoints: No adhesive layer — designed for heat lamination into PVC card bodies, ultrasonic welding into housings, or embedding during injection moulding.
Ultra-thin 50 µm PET substrate (±2 µm thickness control) — survives card lamination temperatures up to 150 °C (PVC) / 180 °C (polycarbonate high-security ID).
Available with all major NXP HF chips — NTAG213/215/216, MIFARE Classic 1K/4K, DESFire EV2/EV3, Ultralight C/EV1, ICODE SLIX2 — chip-type certificate per delivery.

sections.title: What an NFC dry inlay actually is
sections.intro: Peel back the printed card, the overlay and the lamination and what actually answers the phone is deceptively small: an NFC chip flip-chip bonded onto a fine multi-turn loop antenna, etched or wound onto a 50 µm PET web. That is the inlay — a bare sub-component, not a finished card — resonating at 13.56 MHz across the ISO/IEC 14443 and NFC Forum HF band. The loop is a coil, not a UHF dipole; the silicon barely changes between programmes, and the antenna geometry is the part you actually specify for the CR-80 card body.

sections.title: Dry, wet, converted: one inlay, three finish states
sections.intro: The same NFC chip and loop antenna leave the line in one of three finish states, and which one you order is dictated entirely by the process waiting downstream. A dry inlay is the bare feedstock; a wet inlay adds the pressure-sensitive adhesive and release liner a label converter laminates from; a converted inlay is that inlay already built into a finished card, tag or label — at which point it has stopped being a component. This page is the dry state: adhesive-free PET, ready for the lamination press.
bullets: Dry inlay — this page: bare PET film, no adhesive and no release liner; the adhesive-free feedstock a card bureau or moulder builds a finished credential from.
Wet inlay — the same chip and antenna plus a pressure-sensitive adhesive layer and a release liner; a converter peels or laminates it into label stock.
Converted — the inlay already embedded in a finished PVC card, key fob or wristband; at that point it is a credential, not a component.
Same NFC chip and loop antenna in every state — the downstream process, not the silicon, decides which you order.

sections.title: Challenges card manufacturers face when sourcing NFC dry inlays
bullets: Lamination delamination at temperature. A card bureau laminating at 140 °C and 200 psi discovers that competitor dry inlays use an adhesive tie layer that softens and shifts at this temperature, causing chip misalignment in 3-5% of cards and a wave defect in the card surface.

Inlay thickness variation causing uneven card surface. A ±5 µm thickness variation in the PET substrate creates a visible 'bump' over the chip area in the finished card, failing the ISO 7810 surface planarity requirement for bank card production.

Pre-encoding incompatibility with card lamination. Buyers who want pre-encoded inlays discover that some chips require an elevated write voltage that exceeds what the encoding station can supply on a thin dry inlay substrate before lamination.

No prelam sheet option for high-speed lines. A card manufacturer running a high-speed lamination line needs prelam sheets (inlay already sandwiched between two PVC overlays) to reduce handling steps; most dry inlay suppliers only supply bare inlays.

Chip type not confirmed at delivery. A buyer ordering MIFARE DESFire EV3 dry inlays receives a batch where 8% of inlays are EV2 chips substituted by the supplier without notice; the firmware difference causes authentication failures during card personalisation.

sections.title: Per-tap data published from a Proud Tek NFC dry inlay (post-lamination)

dataHighlight.heading: Read distance in CR-80 PVC card body — consumer phone tap
dataHighlight.text: Once laminated into a CR-80 PVC card body, the dry inlay's antenna detunes ≤±5% from the bare-inlay frequency due to PVC dielectric loading. Read distance in the finished card is 3-5 cm with a consumer smartphone (iPhone 7+ / NFC Android) and 5-8 cm with a dedicated ISO 14443 reader (HID Omnikey, ACS, Identiv, FEIG). Antenna Q-factor is optimised for the finished card body, not the bare inlay — buyers laminating the inlay should expect bare-inlay read distance to be lower than post-lamination distance because the card geometry tunes the antenna into resonance. Pre-qualification testing at the buyer's exact press parameters is included with every order.
dataHighlight.source: ISO/IEC 14443 Type A / Type B 13.56 MHz HF proximity air interface; NXP NTAG213/215/216 + MIFARE DESFire EV3 datasheets; brand-deployment data from card-bureau integrators.

sections.title: NFC dry inlay timeline — from PVC card factory to programmable credential

items.label: 1985 — ISO 7810 first edition
items.text: ISO 7810:1985 establishes the CR-80 card dimensions (85.60 × 53.98 × 0.76 mm) and surface planarity baseline that has governed payment + ID + access cards for 40+ years.

items.label: 1996 — MIFARE Classic + ISO/IEC 14443
items.text: Philips (now NXP) launches MIFARE Classic 1K — first widely deployed 13.56 MHz HF contactless smartcard chip; ISO/IEC 14443 Type A air interface ratified internationally.

items.label: 2001 — NFC Forum founded
items.text: NXP, Sony and Nokia found the NFC Forum to standardise short-range tag-based interaction on the same 13.56 MHz frequency family — bridging contactless smartcards and consumer NFC tags.

items.label: 2008-2013 — NTAG family + DESFire EV1/EV2 launch
items.text: NXP introduces NTAG203 → NTAG213/215/216 (NFC Forum Type 2 Tag) and DESFire EV1 → EV2 (AES-128 cryptographic) — full HF chip range that drives demand for adhesive-free dry inlays in card manufacturing.

items.label: 2014 — Apple Pay + global contactless payment
items.text: Apple ships iPhone 6 with NFC for Apple Pay; EMVCo Book D contactless specification matures + contactless-payment-card (DESFire / EMV) volume scales globally.

items.label: 2017 — NFC Forum Type 4 Tag + Apple Core NFC
items.text: Apple iOS 11 introduces Core NFC framework — NFC Forum Type 4 Tag reading on iPhone 7+ becomes consumer-grade. NTAG21x dry inlays in printed-NFC-card form factor see explosive growth.

items.label: 2020-2024 — NFC business cards + healthcare credentials
items.text: NTAG216 dry inlays become default for NFC business cards (Linq / Popl / Mobilo / dot.) — full vCard 4.0 fits without truncation. Healthcare patient-info cards + smart packaging adopt dry inlays at scale.

items.label: 2026 — Today: NFC dry inlay chip-family-anchor for card lamination
items.text: Operating notes from bank-card-bureau, hotel-key-card-manufacturer, corporate-access-badge, key-fob-injection-mould and silicone-wristband-converter programmes converge on NTAG21x / DESFire EV3 / Ultralight C dry inlays + prelam sheet service + chip-type certificate as the default card-lamination architecture.

faq.question: Can dry inlays survive PVC card lamination?
faq.answer: Yes. Our dry inlays are designed for standard PVC lamination at 130-150 °C and 150-300 psi. The PET substrate and chip bonding are rated for these conditions. We recommend testing with your specific lamination press and cycle parameters before production runs — we provide pre-qualification testing reports at the buyer's exact press parameters.

faq.question: What is the minimum order for card-size inlays?
faq.answer: Minimum order is 5,000 inlays. For custom antenna designs or non-standard chip types, minimum may be higher (10,000+). Contact us with your specifications for an exact quote.

faq.question: Do you supply prelam sheets (inlay already laminated between PVC layers)?
faq.answer: Yes. We can supply prelam sheets — the dry inlay already laminated between two thin PVC overlay sheets, ready for your final lamination with printed PVC panels. This reduces your production steps and improves yield. MOQ 10,000 sheets.

faq.question: Which standards govern PVC card construction and NFC / HF chip selection for payment, ID and access credentials?
faq.answer: ISO/IEC 7810:2019 defines the CR-80 card dimensions (85.60 × 53.98 × 0.76 mm) and surface planarity; ISO/IEC 7816 covers contact interface; ISO/IEC 14443 Type A / B defines the 13.56 MHz HF proximity air interface used by MIFARE Classic / DESFire and NTAG families; ISO/IEC 15693 defines vicinity (ICODE SLIX2). For payment cards, EMVCo Contactless Book D adds additional test and certification requirements. Our dry inlays are supplied in CR-80 geometry with antenna designs tuned for ISO 14443 Type A or Type B as specified, and we can provide inlays qualified for EMVCo Book D contactless payment card builds on request.

faq.question: How do card bureau lamination cycles (temperature, pressure, dwell) affect chip survival and NDEF retention?
faq.answer: Standard PVC lamination runs 140-150 °C at 200-300 psi for 15-25 minutes dwell on hydraulic platen presses (Bürkle, Wickert, Agfa); polycarbonate lamination for high-security IDs runs hotter (160-180 °C) with longer dwell. NXP NTAG and MIFARE chips are rated for these cycles per the datasheets, but pre-encoded NDEF or DESFire application keys must be written after lamination curing if the cycle exceeds the chip's data-retention reflow spec. We pre-qualify our dry inlays at the buyer's exact press parameters and supply a lamination compatibility report; for pre-encoded programmes we recommend post-lamination encoding via the card personalisation line.
